[Interview, 2006-09-27, All Things Considered]
HOST: Give us, if you could, to start this off, the lay of the land.
GUEST: The lay of the land is this focus on the six seats Democrats need to take the majority. Today, I think there are six Senate races out there that are too close to call that are held by Republicans. By contrast, Democrats only have one seat that they are in real danger of losing. You know, it's not hard for me to see how Democrats get three seats, four seats, five seats. That sixth seat will be a little harder. They need almost everything to go right for them on election night.

HOST: Tick through the six seats for us.
GUEST: Conrad Burns in Montana. That's what we just heard. Rick Santorum of Pennsylvania, Mike Dewine in Ohio, Lincoln Chafee in Rhode Island, Jim Talent in Missouri and then the open seat in Tennessee, where Bill Frist is retiring. For Democrats, their one real endangered seat, believe it or not, is in the very blue state of New Jersey.

HOST: Bob Menendez is now under investigation, running against a candidate with a quite familiar name in that region.
GUEST: That's right. You know, Menendez was appointed to the Senate in December by Jon Corzine, who won the governor's race. Tom Kean, Jr. is the Republican. He's a state senator obviously. His father was a very, very popular governor. His most recent position was co-chair of the 9/11 Commission. Now, the Kean name carries a great deal of cache. And Menendez, as you noted, has some of his own problems. Not only is he under investigation, but scandal seems to be kicking up in other places around the state.

HOST: That's what I wondered. I wondered if voters there might be feeling a bit of scandal fatigue. The former governor, Jim McGreevy, is out right now hawking his book.
GUEST: That's right. There was a state senator who pleaded guilty a couple of weeks ago to corruption. There are rumors of more indictments. Even in New Jersey, they might hit scandal fatigue. But I have to tell you, New Jersey's very blue state and Republicans have struggled there in good political environments for them. This is not a good environment. But looking at the data, you know, consistently over the last three or four months, Tom Kean is more than holding his own here.

[Interview, 2006-09-27, All Things Considered]
HOST: GUEST: Thank you.

[Interview, 2006-10-16, All Things Considered]
HOST: Joining us to talk about this are GUEST, who is the Senate expert for The Cook Political Report. Welcome back to the program, GUEST.
GUEST: (The Cook Political Report): Thank you.

HOST: And Chuck Todd, who's editor in chief of the online political digest Hotline. Welcomes to the program, Chuck Todd.

HOST: Firs the House, Chuck. What is the informed view nowadays of how close the race is for a majority of the House of Representatives in November?

HOST: I just want you to pursue your geographical division of America into inside the Beltway, that is in and around Washington, D.C., and the rest of the country. Were state political operatives any more sensitive to this? Were they aware of what was going on?

HOST: There are three more weeks of campaigning, and in many states, the candidates either for senator or governor have had their big debates already. GUEST, what does experience tell you about how much motion there might be typically in the last three weeks of a non-presidential election year? Can it be a lot?
GUEST: Well, I think, you know, in these close races, certainly. What is left to do is, you know, the final attacks back and forth, trying to score some points there, and then it is getting your voters out to the polls. You know, Democrats, especially in Senate races this year, feel that they have put, you know, an operation on the ground to do that, to sort of go head to head with Republicans' very successful turnout operation over the last two elections. This is pretty much what goes on in the last three weeks.

HOST: I'm curious to hear from both of you before I let you go. Congressman Foley's problems may have dominated the news for a week or so, but does this election - is it likely to go down as the Iraq election? What do you think, Chuck Todd?

HOST: GUEST?
GUEST: Now only is about Iraq, but as mid-term elections tend to be, this is also a referendum on President Bush and his policies on Iraq, on national security, on the economy. You know, this is what mid-term elections are about. They are referendums on the party in power.

HOST: Well, thanks to both of you for talking politics with us today. GUEST of The Cook Political Report and Chuck Todd of the Hotline. Thanks.
GUEST: Thank you.
